Secondary internet gateways only transmit black-and-white images.
The web server's hard drive will freeze.
The client's web browser will automatically uninstall itself.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: TCP connections are strictly identified by 5-tuples. The client initiated a session to public IP 10.0.2.15. If the server's reply bypasses the firewall and leaves via another router, the packet is not de-translated and arrives with source IP 172.16.50.10. The client's TCP stack drops it immediately as unsolicited. Options B, C, and D are incorrect.

concepts.purpose: Analyze Destination NAT (DNAT) mechanics, Port Forwarding, and return path symmetry.
howItWorks: Rewrites destination IP on ingress; state table reverses translation on return.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Configured in pfSense under Firewall -> NAT -> Port Forward.

concepts.title: Firewall Management-Plane Security: Control Plane Hardening & Access Control
learningObjectives: Differentiate the Data Plane (packet forwarding) from the Management Plane (firewall administration).
Apply management-plane hardening: binding to dedicated MGMT interfaces, disabling WAN management, and enforcing HTTPS/SSH.
Understand Anti-Lockout rules and out-of-band administration best practices.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: The Management Plane is the administrative brain of the firewall—controlling the webConfigurator GUI, SSH shell, console menus, and configuration databases. If an attacker gains access to the management plane, they own the entire network: they can disable firewall rules, inspect encrypted tunnels, and pivot into internal servers. Securing the management plane through strict interface binding and hardening is the first duty of every firewall administrator.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
Management Plane Hardening Pillars: 
1) Interface Isolation: Management daemons (lighttpd webConfigurator and sshd) must NEVER listen on or be reachable from the untrusted WAN interface. They should strictly bind to a dedicated out-of-band Management subnet (192.168.100.0/24) or internal LAN.
2) Strong Cryptography: Disable plain HTTP and unencrypted Telnet completely. Enforce TLS 1.3 for web access and modern ED25519 / RSA-4096 keys for SSH.
3) Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Require Time-based One-Time Passwords (TOTP) or hardware tokens for all administrator logins.
4) Anti-Lockout Rules: pfSense includes a built-in anti-lockout rule on the LAN interface to prevent administrators from accidentally locking themselves out while editing rules. In hardened production environments, this rule is relocated to a dedicated MGMT interface.
5) Rate Limiting & Brute-Force Defense: Enforce maximum login failure thresholds to lock out automated credential-stuffing attacks.
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         FIREWALL PLANE SEPARATION                             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
[ DATA PLANE: High-Speed Packet Forwarding ]
WAN Interface (em0) <======== (Transit Traffic) ========> LAN (em1) / DMZ (em2)
                 | (Strictly Blocks Port 443/22 to Firewall)
                 v
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
[ MANAGEMENT PLANE: Dedicated Administrative Control ]
+-----------------------------------+
| pfSense webConfigurator (Port 443)|
| Secure Shell Daemon (Port 22)     | <=== [ MGMT Workstation: 192.168.100.10 ]
| System Console Menu (TTY / Vbox)  |      (Only authorized IP subnet permitted!)
+-----------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In our training architecture, pfSense assigns Adapter 4 to a dedicated MGMT zone (192.168.100.1/24). Web GUI and SSH access are permitted exclusively from the Administrator Workstation on 192.168.100.10. If a compromised machine on LAN (10.10.10.50) or DMZ (172.16.50.10) attempts to browse 'https://192.168.100.1', pfSense drops the connection immediately.
concepts.configurationRelevance: In pfSense CE under System -> Advanced -> Admin Access: 1) Protocol is set to HTTPS, 2) TCP Port is set to 443 (or custom port), 3) SSH is enabled with key-based authentication, 4) Under System -> User Manager, default 'admin' password is changed, and 5) Anti-lockout rule is reviewed.
concepts.verification: From WAN tester, run 'nmap -p 22,80,443 10.0.2.15'. Confirm all ports report 'filtered'. From MGMT workstation (192.168.100.10), browse 'https://192.168.100.1' and verify the pfSense login page renders cleanly over TLS.
commonMistakes: Leaving default administrative credentials ('admin / pfsense') active after initial installation.
Creating a firewall rule permitting WAN to access port 443 on the firewall interface to allow 'working from home' without a VPN.
Disabling the anti-lockout rule before creating a valid management permit rule on another interface, locking yourself out of the firewall.
concepts.troubleshooting: If you accidentally lock yourself out of the pfSense webConfigurator, connect to the VirtualBox VM console screen and select Option 15 (Restore recent configuration) or Option 8 (Shell) to run 'pfctl -d' to temporarily disable the packet filter.
keyTakeaways: The Management Plane controls the firewall and must be separated from data transit paths.
Never expose webConfigurator (port 443) or SSH (port 22) to the untrusted WAN interface.
Enforce out-of-band management subnets, strong cryptographic keys, and MFA.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the single most dangerous configuration mistake an administrator can make regarding firewall management-plane security?
options: Creating an allow rule on the WAN interface permitting any external Internet IP to access the webConfigurator (port 443) with default credentials.
Changing the firewall hostname to something funny.
Backing up the configuration to an encrypted USB drive.
Configuring NTP time synchronization.

concepts.title: Common Enterprise Firewall Design & Architecture Mistakes
learningObjectives: Identify the ten most frequent enterprise firewall design and configuration errors.
Analyze the risks of Rule Shadowing, Any-Any permits, missing egress filtering, and flat networks.
Implement audit checklists and policy hygiene workflows to maintain a hardened firewall posture.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: Firewalls are sophisticated, powerful security instruments, but they are only as effective as the human engineers who configure them. A single misordered rule, an overly broad permit statement, or a forgotten testing rule can completely nullify a multi-million-dollar cybersecurity investment. Reviewing common firewall design mistakes is critical to avoiding catastrophic security breaches.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The Top 7 Critical Firewall Mistakes: 
1) Rule Shadowing: Placing a broad rule (e.g. 'Pass Any to Any') above a specific restriction, causing the specific rule to never be evaluated.
2) Permissive Egress Filtering: Leaving 'LAN to Any' completely unrestricted, allowing infected internal endpoints to establish outbound command-and-control (C2) reverse shells.
3) Public Servers on LAN: Putting web or mail servers directly inside the trusted LAN rather than an isolated DMZ.
4) Management on WAN: Exposing administrative interfaces to the Internet for remote convenience without a VPN.
5) Orphan & Zombie Rules: Leaving temporary rules created for troubleshooting active permanently in production.
6) Missing Logging: Failing to enable logging on drop rules, rendering intrusion forensics impossible.
7) Flat Architecture: Failing to segment internal networks, allowing ransomware to pivot across all departments.
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     CRITICAL FIREWALL DESIGN PITFALLS                         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
[ P1: RULE SHADOWING ]
  Rule 1: PASS Source: LAN_Net, Dest: ANY, Port: ANY <--- (Matches everything!)
  Rule 2: BLOCK Source: LAN_Net, Dest: Ransomware_IP <--- (SHADOWED! Never evaluated!)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[ P2: MISSING EGRESS FILTERING ]
  Malware infected PC: Connects outbound on port 4444 (Reverse Shell)
  Firewall with 'Default Allow LAN to Any' forwards packet without objection!
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[ P3: UNSEGMENTED FLAT NETWORK ]
  Public Web Server compromised -> Attacker scans LAN directly across Layer 2 switch!
concepts.enterpriseExample: In our training review, we audit a sample pfSense ruleset containing a shadowed rule: an admin placed 'Allow LAN to Any' on line 1, and 'Block LAN to BadSite' on line 2. Students test accessing BadSite and observe that traffic is permitted because pfSense stops evaluation on the first match (line 1), demonstrating the danger of rule misordering live.
concepts.configurationRelevance: In pfSense CE, rule ordering is managed via drag-and-drop under Firewall -> Rules. Administrators can drag specific block rules above broad permit rules and click 'Save' followed by 'Apply Changes'. Under Status -> Filter Reload, ruleset syntax is validated.
concepts.verification: Conduct a rule audit: verify no 'Pass Any to Any' rule exists above specific restrictions. Verify DMZ rules block traffic to LAN net. Verify WAN rules contain zero management port permits.
commonMistakes: Believing a rule at line 10 will take effect if a rule at line 2 already matched the packet.
Failing to document the business purpose of rules using pfSense's 'Description' field.
Creating broad port ranges instead of utilizing named port aliases.
concepts.troubleshooting: If a newly created blocking rule fails to block traffic, check the rule order: if an earlier rule matches the same traffic, drag the blocking rule above it and clear active states in Diagnostics -> States.
keyTakeaways: Rule shadowing occurs when an earlier broad rule renders subsequent rules useless.
Strict egress filtering and DMZ isolation are mandatory for enterprise defense.
Regular ruleset auditing and policy hygiene prevent configuration drift.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is 'Rule Shadowing' in a firewall configuration?
options: A condition where a broader rule earlier in the ruleset matches all packets intended for a more specific rule below it, rendering the specific rule completely ineffective.
A rule that creates an encrypted shadow copy of network packets.
A firewall rule that only runs during nighttime hours.
A rule stored in the cloud as a backup.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: Rule Shadowing occurs when a rule placed earlier in the list matches the same traffic criteria as a subsequent rule. Because firewalls stop processing on the first match, the lower rule is 'shadowed' and will never be evaluated. Options B, C, and D are incorrect.

concepts.title: VirtualBox Networking Modes Compared: NAT, Bridged, Host-Only, and Internal Network
learningObjectives: Compare the four core VirtualBox networking modes: NAT, Bridged, Host-Only, and Internal Network.
Understand why Internal Network mode provides absolute hypervisor-level isolation for virtual security zones.
Choose the correct adapter mode for each virtual firewall interface in a multi-zone security lab.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: When virtualizing an enterprise firewall inside Oracle VirtualBox, the hypervisor's virtual network adapter modes dictate how virtual network interfaces communicate with each other, with the host machine, and with the external Internet. Selecting the wrong virtual networking mode can cause IP address conflicts on your physical network, expose unhardened virtual interfaces directly to the local LAN, or inadvertently bridge isolated security zones together, invalidating the firewall's perimeter security.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
VirtualBox provides four primary networking modes:
1. NAT (Network Address Translation): VirtualBox creates an internal router/DHCP server on subnet 10.0.2.0/24. The VM initiates outbound connections translated to the host's IP address. Inbound connections from the host or external network are blocked unless explicit port forwarding is configured.
2. Bridged Adapter: The virtual NIC binds directly to a physical network adapter on the host (Ethernet or Wi-Fi). The VM appears as an independent physical device on the host's physical network, receiving an IP from the physical router's DHCP server.
3. Host-Only Adapter: Creates a private software-defined network shared strictly between the host operating system and selected VMs. No external Internet access is possible unless routed through the host.
4. Internal Network: Creates an isolated, virtual Layer 2 software switch entirely contained within VirtualBox memory. Only VMs explicitly assigned to the same Internal Network name (e.g., 'sxl-lan') can communicate with each other. The host OS has zero visibility into this network, and there is zero external access unless a router/firewall (like pfSense) is connected to it.
concepts.enterpriseExample: In our enterprise lab architecture, pfSense uses NAT mode on Adapter 1 (WAN) to safely obtain outbound Internet access without interfering with the host's physical LAN. For Adapters 2, 3, and 4 (LAN, DMZ, MGMT), we use Internal Network mode with distinct network names ('sxl-lan', 'sxl-dmz', 'sxl-mgmt'). This ensures that virtual machines in different zones can ONLY communicate by sending packets through the pfSense firewall interfaces.
concepts.configurationRelevance:
In VirtualBox VM Settings -> Network:
- Adapter 1: Attached to 'NAT'
- Adapter 2: Attached to 'Internal Network', Name: 'sxl-lan', Promiscuous Mode: 'Allow VMs'
- Adapter 3: Attached to 'Internal Network', Name: 'sxl-dmz', Promiscuous Mode: 'Allow VMs'
- Adapter 4: Attached to 'Internal Network', Name: 'sxl-mgmt', Promiscuous Mode: 'Allow VMs'
concepts.verification: Run 'VBoxManage showvminfo sxl-pfsense-fw01 | grep -i "NIC "' in terminal or check VM Settings -> Network in the VirtualBox GUI. Confirm each adapter has the designated attachment mode and correct internal network name.
commonMistakes: Setting LAN or DMZ adapters to 'Bridged', exposing virtual lab DHCP servers to your physical home or office network and disrupting physical devices.
Typing different Internal Network names on the firewall and client VM (e.g., 'sxl-lan' on pfSense but 'lan' on the Ubuntu client), creating separate isolated virtual switches with no connectivity.
Leaving Adapter 1 unattached or setting it to Internal Network, preventing pfSense from downloading package updates or routing outbound Internet traffic.
concepts.troubleshooting: If a LAN client cannot reach pfSense at 10.10.10.1, verify that both the pfSense Adapter 2 and the client's Adapter 1 are attached to 'Internal Network' with the exact, case-sensitive name 'sxl-lan'.
keyTakeaways: NAT mode connects a VM out to the Internet while hiding it behind the hypervisor's translation engine.
Internal Network mode creates isolated virtual Layer 2 switches inside VirtualBox memory.
Assigning distinct Internal Network names creates physically isolated security zones enforced at the hypervisor level.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is 'Internal Network' mode used for LAN, DMZ, and MGMT adapters in our virtual firewall lab instead of 'Bridged' mode?
options: Internal Network mode ensures virtual traffic is completely isolated inside hypervisor memory, preventing virtual DHCP servers from interfering with the physical network and forcing all inter-zone traffic through the firewall.
Internal Network mode is 10 times faster than Bridged mode because it skips TCP checksum validation.
Bridged mode does not support IPv4 addresses, only IPv6.
VirtualBox only allows one virtual machine to use Bridged mode at a time.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: Internal Network mode isolates virtual traffic to software-defined Layer 2 switches within VirtualBox. This prevents virtual DHCP servers from colliding with physical networks and guarantees all inter-zone traffic is mediated by the firewall. Options B, C, and D are false.

concepts.title: Lab Topology Blueprint: 4 Zones, 4 Interfaces, IP Plan, Subnet Masks and Gateway Assignments
learningObjectives: Review the complete four-zone enterprise addressing scheme for the ShadowXLab firewall lab.
Understand interface names, IP assignments, CIDR subnet masks, and default gateway roles for each zone.
Identify the role of each client and server endpoint in the multi-zone architecture.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: A successful firewall deployment requires a meticulously documented IP addressing plan before any installation begins. In our enterprise scenario, the organisation deploys a dedicated perimeter firewall (hostname: `sxl-pfsense-fw01`) connecting four distinct operational zones: WAN (untrusted external network), LAN (internal user workstations), DMZ (public-facing application servers), and MGMT (secure out-of-band administration network).
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The complete addressing scheme and interface allocation is defined as follows:
1. WAN Interface (vtnet0 / em0):
   - Attachment: VirtualBox NAT Network
   - IP Address: DHCP assigned (typically 10.0.2.15/24)
   - Default Gateway: 10.0.2.2 (VirtualBox virtual gateway)
   - Trust Level: Untrusted (External / Internet)
2. LAN Interface (vtnet1 / em1):
   - Attachment: Internal Network 'sxl-lan'
   - Firewall IP: 10.10.10.1/24 (Subnet: 10.10.10.0/24)
   - Client Pool: 10.10.10.100 - 10.10.10.200 (DHCP enabled)
   - Client Workstation: 10.10.10.10/24, Gateway: 10.10.10.1
   - Trust Level: High (Internal Corporate Network)
3. DMZ Interface (vtnet2 / em2):
   - Attachment: Internal Network 'sxl-dmz'
   - Firewall IP: 172.16.50.1/24 (Subnet: 172.16.50.0/24)
   - DMZ Web Server: 172.16.50.10/24 (Static), Gateway: 172.16.50.1
   - Trust Level: Low / Semi-Trusted (Public Services)
4. MGMT Interface (vtnet3 / em3):
   - Attachment: Internal Network 'sxl-mgmt'
   - Firewall IP: 192.168.100.1/24 (Subnet: 192.168.100.0/24)
   - Admin Workstation: 192.168.100.10/24 (Static), Gateway: 192.168.100.1
   - Trust Level: Isolated Out-of-Band Administrative Network
concepts.enterpriseExample: In an enterprise data center, the firewall is the default gateway for every endpoint in the company. Workstations on 10.10.10.0/24 configure 10.10.10.1 as their gateway. When a client at 10.10.10.10 sends a packet to the DMZ web server at 172.16.50.10, the client checks its local subnet mask (/24), recognizes the destination is remote, and forwards the packet directly to 10.10.10.1 for firewall inspection.
concepts.configurationRelevance: This blueprint forms the contract for the entire lab. During pfSense console setup and webGUI configuration, these exact interface names, IP addresses, and subnet masks must be entered without deviation.
concepts.verification: Document the IP table on your lab worksheet. Verify each subnet uses non-overlapping private IP address space (RFC 1918) and that the firewall IP is assigned the first usable host address (.1) in each subnet.
commonMistakes: Using overlapping subnets (e.g., assigning 10.10.10.1/24 to LAN and 10.10.10.1/24 to DMZ), causing fatal routing conflicts in the BSD kernel.
Using a /16 or /8 mask inadvertently (e.g., 10.10.10.1/8), which encompasses the entire Class A network and causes pfSense to treat external networks as local.
Setting client default gateways to their own IP address rather than the firewall's interface IP.
concepts.troubleshooting: If a host cannot route traffic, verify its subnet mask: 'ip -4 addr show' on Linux or 'Get-NetIPAddress' in PowerShell. Ensure the gateway matches pfSense's IP on that specific interface.
keyTakeaways: Each firewall interface connects to exactly one unique, non-overlapping subnet.
The firewall serves as the default gateway for all endpoints attached to its internal interfaces.
Pre-planning IP subnets and interface roles prevents routing loops and configuration deadlocks.

knowledgeCheck.question: In our approved lab topology, which IP address and subnet mask are assigned to the pfSense DMZ interface?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: In the ShadowXLab enterprise architecture, the DMZ interface is assigned 172.16.50.1/24 (subnet 172.16.50.0/24). LAN is 10.10.10.1/24, MGMT is 192.168.100.1/24, and WAN is 10.0.2.15/24 via VirtualBox NAT.

concepts.title: Creating the pfSense VM: RAM, CPU, Disk Sizing, and FreeBSD 64-bit OS Selection
learningObjectives: Configure a new VirtualBox virtual machine with appropriate hardware specifications for pfSense Community Edition.
Select the correct operating system family (BSD) and version (FreeBSD 64-bit) for kernel compatibility.
Allocate RAM, virtual CPUs, and virtual hard disk storage balanced for training performance.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: pfSense Community Edition (CE) is built upon the FreeBSD Unix operating system. When provisioning a virtual machine for pfSense in VirtualBox, selecting the correct operating system profile ensures that VirtualBox enables appropriate hardware virtualization extensions (VT-x/AMD-V), ACPI support, and optimal network driver emulation. Sizing the VM correctly guarantees responsive webGUI operations without over-committing the host computer's resources.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The virtual machine provisioning specifications are:
1. Name: `sxl-pfsense-fw01`
2. Type: `BSD`
3. Version: `FreeBSD (64-bit)`
4. Memory (RAM): Minimum 1024 MB (1 GB), recommended 2048 MB (2 GB) for classroom labs. pfSense's base system requires ~512 MB, with remaining memory used for PHP-FPM webGUI processes and packet filter state tables.
5. Processors (vCPU): 1 vCPU is sufficient for standard lab routing; 2 vCPUs are recommended if testing traffic generation or VPN encryption.
6. Hard Disk: 16 GB to 20 GB dynamically allocated VDI (VirtualBox Disk Image). pfSense installs in under 3 GB; the remaining disk provides space for system logs, packet captures, and package caches.
7. Optical Drive: Attach the official `pfSense-CE-2.7.x-RELEASE-amd64.iso` image to the virtual SATA/IDE controller.
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| VirtualBox VM Provisioning Wizard: sxl-pfsense-fw01                   |
|                                                                       |
|  OS Type:        BSD                                                  |
|  Version:        FreeBSD (64-bit)                                     |
|  Base Memory:    2048 MB (2 GB)                                       |
|  Processors:     2 vCPUs (Hardware Virtualization Enabled)            |
|  Boot Order:     Optical, Hard Disk (Floppy disabled)                |
|  Storage:        20 GB VDI Dynamically Allocated Disk                 |
|  Optical Disk:   pfSense-CE-2.7.2-RELEASE-amd64.iso                   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In production bare-metal or enterprise hypervisor (ESXi/Proxmox) environments, sizing is based on expected throughput and concurrent connection state counts. Each state table entry consumes approximately 1 KB of RAM. A 2 GB RAM allocation supports up to 1,000,000 concurrent state table sessions, far exceeding classroom lab requirements.
concepts.configurationRelevance: In VirtualBox: Click 'New', enter Name: `sxl-pfsense-fw01`, select Type: `BSD`, Version: `FreeBSD (64-bit)`. In the System tab, verify 'Enable EFI' is UNCHECKED (pfSense CE standard ISO uses BIOS MBR/ZFS boot by default in standard lab profiles). In Storage tab, verify the ISO is mounted.
concepts.verification: Check VM Settings -> System. Confirm Base Memory displays 2048 MB, Processors displays 2, and the acceleration tab shows VT-x/AMD-V enabled. Check Storage tab to confirm pfSense ISO is mounted in the optical drive.
commonMistakes: Selecting 'Linux' or 'Windows' as OS Type instead of 'BSD / FreeBSD (64-bit)', leading to kernel panics or missing storage drivers during boot.
Enabling 'EFI' checkbox when using an MBR-based ISO image, causing the VM to boot into an interactive EFI shell instead of the pfSense installer.
Allocating less than 512 MB RAM, resulting in PHP out-of-memory crashes during webGUI initialization.
concepts.troubleshooting: If the VM drops into 'UEFI Interactive Shell v2.2', power off the VM, open Settings -> System -> Motherboard, uncheck 'Enable EFI (special OSes only)', and power on the VM again.
keyTakeaways: pfSense CE runs on FreeBSD 64-bit and requires the BSD/FreeBSD VirtualBox OS profile.
2048 MB RAM and 2 vCPUs provide optimal performance for training exercises.
Standard ISO boot requires legacy BIOS mode (EFI disabled) in VirtualBox.

concepts.title: Virtual Network Adapter Assignment: 4 Interfaces for WAN, LAN, DMZ, and MGMT
learningObjectives: Configure four distinct virtual network adapters in VirtualBox for the pfSense VM.
Map Adapter 1 to WAN (NAT) and Adapters 2, 3, 4 to Internal Networks.
Understand virtual adapter driver types (Intel PRO/1000 MT Desktop vs VirtIO) and promiscuous mode settings.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: By default, VirtualBox enables only a single network adapter on newly created virtual machines. Because pfSense acts as a multi-zone router and firewall, administrators must enable and configure four distinct network adapters in the VM settings before powering on the machine for installation.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
pfSense identifies physical network cards using FreeBSD driver prefixes (such as `em0`, `em1`, `em2`, `em3` for Intel PRO/1000 adapters, or `vtnet0`, `vtnet1`, `vtnet2`, `vtnet3` for Paravirtualized VirtIO adapters). In VirtualBox, we configure:
- Adapter 1:
  * Enable Network Adapter: Checked
  * Attached to: NAT
  * Adapter Type: Intel PRO/1000 MT Desktop (82540EM)
  * Role: WAN (connects to VirtualBox NAT engine at 10.0.2.15)
- Adapter 2:
  * Enable Network Adapter: Checked
  * Attached to: Internal Network
  * Name: `sxl-lan`
  * Adapter Type: Intel PRO/1000 MT Desktop (82540EM)
  * Promiscuous Mode: Allow VMs
  * Role: LAN (connects to 10.10.10.0/24 client switch)
- Adapter 3:
  * Enable Network Adapter: Checked
  * Attached to: Internal Network
  * Name: `sxl-dmz`
  * Adapter Type: Intel PRO/1000 MT Desktop (82540EM)
  * Promiscuous Mode: Allow VMs
  * Role: DMZ (connects to 172.16.50.0/24 server switch)
- Adapter 4:
  * Enable Network Adapter: Checked
  * Attached to: Internal Network
  * Name: `sxl-mgmt`
  * Adapter Type: Intel PRO/1000 MT Desktop (82540EM)
  * Promiscuous Mode: Allow VMs
  * Role: MGMT (connects to 192.168.100.0/24 management switch)
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| VirtualBox Network Settings: sxl-pfsense-fw01                                     |
|                                                                                   |
|  [Tab: Adapter 1] -> [x] Enable | Attached to: NAT                                |
|  [Tab: Adapter 2] -> [x] Enable | Attached to: Internal Network | Name: sxl-lan   |
|  [Tab: Adapter 3] -> [x] Enable | Attached to: Internal Network | Name: sxl-dmz   |
|  [Tab: Adapter 4] -> [x] Enable | Attached to: Internal Network | Name: sxl-mgmt  |
|                                                                                   |
|  Hardware mapping in FreeBSD:                                                     |
|  Adapter 1 -> em0 / vtnet0 (WAN)                                                  |
|  Adapter 2 -> em1 / vtnet1 (LAN)                                                  |
|  Adapter 3 -> em2 / vtnet2 (OPT1 / DMZ)                                           |
|  Adapter 4 -> em3 / vtnet3 (OPT2 / MGMT)                                          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In an enterprise physical appliance (such as a Netgate 6100 or 8200), physical RJ-45 or SFP+ ports are labeled WAN, LAN, OPT1, OPT2. In VirtualBox, the four adapter tabs correspond directly to these physical chassis ports.
concepts.configurationRelevance: Open VirtualBox -> Select `sxl-pfsense-fw01` -> Settings -> Network. Walk through Adapter tabs 1 through 4, ensuring each adapter is enabled with its exact mode and network name before booting.
concepts.verification: Review the summary in VirtualBox VM details panel under 'Network': Confirm Adapter 1 is NAT, and Adapters 2-4 display 'Internal Network, 'sxl-lan'', 'sxl-dmz'', 'sxl-mgmt''.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to check the 'Enable Network Adapter' checkbox on Adapters 3 and 4, causing pfSense to only detect two interfaces on boot.
Inconsistent naming of internal networks (e.g., using 'sxl_lan' with underscore vs 'sxl-lan' with hyphen), which creates separate isolated broadcast domains.
Selecting different adapter types across interfaces (mixing PCnet-FAST III and Intel PRO/1000), which results in different FreeBSD driver names (le0 vs em0).
concepts.troubleshooting: If pfSense boots and only shows two interfaces (em0 and em1), shut down the VM and verify that Adapters 3 and 4 have 'Enable Network Adapter' checked in VirtualBox.
keyTakeaways: All four virtual adapters must be enabled before installing pfSense.
Adapter 1 connects to NAT for outbound WAN transit.
Adapters 2, 3, and 4 connect to distinct named Internal Networks for LAN, DMZ, and MGMT isolation.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the consequence of configuring Adapter 3 and Adapter 4 with the same Internal Network name (e.g., 'sxl-lan') instead of distinct names?
options: DMZ and MGMT will be bridged onto the same Layer 2 virtual switch as LAN, completely bypassing firewall isolation between those zones.
VirtualBox will crash immediately upon powering on the VM.
pfSense will automatically assign the same IP address to both interfaces.
The network adapters will disable themselves automatically.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: VirtualBox uses the Internal Network name as a virtual switch identifier. If multiple adapters share the same name, they are plugged into the same virtual switch, merging the broadcast domains and eliminating perimeter firewall boundaries between zones.

concepts.purpose: Configure the 4 virtual network adapters in VirtualBox to represent WAN, LAN, DMZ, and MGMT.
howItWorks: Maps hypervisor adapter tabs to FreeBSD em0-em3 network interface cards.

concepts.title: pfSense CE Installation: ISO Boot, Keymap, Filesystem Selection (ZFS vs UFS), and Reboot
learningObjectives: Boot the pfSense Community Edition installer from ISO inside Oracle VirtualBox.
Navigate the text-based BSD installer dialogs (Accept Copyright, Install pfSense, Keymap).
Evaluate ZFS (recommended for modern systems) versus UFS filesystems and execute installation.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: Installing pfSense Community Edition involves running the FreeBSD-based text installer. Unlike graphical operating system installers, pfSense uses an ncurses menu system controlled via keyboard navigation (Arrow keys, Spacebar, Enter, and Tab). Understanding the installer options—particularly filesystem selection between ZFS and legacy UFS—ensures a reliable, crash-resilient installation.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The installation sequence progresses through distinct stages:
1. Boot Loader: The VM boots from the ISO. At the ASCII pfSense logo prompt, press Enter or wait 3 seconds for default multi-user kernel boot.
2. Copyright Notice: Press Enter to 'Accept' the Netgate copyright and trademark notices.
3. Distribution Selection: Choose 'Install pfSense' and press Enter (do not select 'Rescue Shell' or 'Recover config.xml').
4. Keymap Selection: Select 'Continue with default keymap' (US keymap) or select your regional keyboard layout.
5. Partitioning / Filesystem:
   - Auto (ZFS): Recommended for modern installations. Provides copy-on-write integrity, boot environments, and protection against power-loss corruption.
   - Auto (UFS): Legacy Unix File System. Lightweight, suitable for low-spec systems or older virtual disks.
   In our lab, select 'Auto (ZFS)', then 'Install -> Stripe - No Redundancy' (single virtual disk `da0`), select the disk with Spacebar `[*] da0`, and press OK.
6. Final Confirmation: Select 'YES' to proceed with disk destruction and installation.
7. Reboot Prompt: Once files are copied, select 'No' to manual shell configuration, select 'Reboot', and immediately unmount the ISO from VirtualBox so the VM boots from the newly installed virtual hard drive.
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Netgate pfSense CE Installer Flow                                     |
|                                                                       |
|  [Boot from ISO]                                                      |
|         |                                                             |
|         v                                                             |
|  [Accept Copyright] -> [Install pfSense] -> [Keymap Selection]        |
|                                                       |               |
|                                                       v               |
|                                            [Filesystem: Auto (ZFS)]   |
|                                                       |               |
|                                                       v               |
|                                            [Pool: Stripe - da0]       |
|                                                       |               |
|                                                       v               |
|  [System Reboot] <------------------------- [Extract & Write Base]    |
|         |                                                             |
|         v (Unmount ISO from VirtualBox Optical Drive)                 |
|  [First Boot from Virtual Hard Disk da0]                              |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In production enterprise appliances, Netgate hardware uses ZFS with mirrored NVMe storage. If an administrator pulls the power plug during an unexpected power outage, ZFS guarantees file system consistency without requiring hours of manual fsck (filesystem check) repairs.
concepts.configurationRelevance: Installer navigation requires using Spacebar to check selection boxes: in the ZFS drive selection dialog, the cursor must be over `da0`, you must press Spacebar to turn `[ ]` into `[*]`, and then press Enter to continue.
concepts.verification: After reboot, observe the VirtualBox console. The pfSense ASCII banner should appear, displaying system version (e.g. pfSense CE 2.7.2-RELEASE), memory statistics, and the interface configuration menu.
commonMistakes: Failing to press Spacebar on `da0` in the ZFS disk selection menu, resulting in an error stating 'No disks selected for pool'.
Leaving the ISO attached in VirtualBox, causing the VM to boot back into the installer instead of loading from the virtual hard disk.
Selecting 'Rescue Shell' at the initial menu, which drops into a command prompt instead of installing.
concepts.troubleshooting: If the installer repeatedly appears after reboot, click Devices -> Optical Drives -> Remove disk from virtual drive, or change the boot order in VM Settings -> System to place Hard Disk first.
keyTakeaways: Use Spacebar to toggle checkbox selections in the BSD installer.
ZFS Stripe mode is ideal for single-disk virtual machines.
Always unmount the installation ISO before the first system reboot.

knowledgeCheck.question: During the pfSense ZFS disk selection step, which keyboard key must be pressed to select the virtual hard drive (da0)?
options: Spacebar (to place an asterisk [*] in the checkbox next to the drive)
Enter (to immediately proceed)
Escape (to exit the menu)
Tab (to highlight the drive)
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: In the BSD ncurses installer dialogs, pressing Spacebar toggles the selection box `[*]`. Pressing Enter without pressing Spacebar first will trigger a 'No disks selected' error.

concepts.purpose: Provide clear step-by-step guidance for installing pfSense CE with ZFS on VirtualBox.
howItWorks: Extracts FreeBSD base system and pfSense PHP engine to the virtual disk.

concepts.title: Initial Console Boot: Interface Detection, VLAN Configuration Prompt, and Physical Mapping
learningObjectives: Understand the interactive prompts presented on the pfSense console during first boot.
Respond correctly to the 'Should VLANs be set up now?' question.
Identify how FreeBSD hardware interface names (em0, em1, em2, em3) correspond to VirtualBox network adapters.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: When pfSense boots for the very first time on a fresh installation, it probes the PCI bus for network interface cards (NICs) and determines that no configuration file (`config.xml`) exists. It halts the boot sequence and launches an interactive console wizard asking whether 802.1Q Virtual LANs (VLANs) should be configured and how physical NICs should be assigned to WAN and LAN roles.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The initial console interface prompt sequence:
1. Interface Inventory: The kernel prints detected network interfaces:
   - `em0` (MAC: 08:00:27:xx:xx:01) -> Adapter 1 (NAT)
   - `em1` (MAC: 08:00:27:xx:xx:02) -> Adapter 2 (Internal 'sxl-lan')
   - `em2` (MAC: 08:00:27:xx:xx:03) -> Adapter 3 (Internal 'sxl-dmz')
   - `em3` (MAC: 08:00:27:xx:xx:04) -> Adapter 4 (Internal 'sxl-mgmt')
2. VLAN Prompt: pfSense asks: `Should VLANs be set up now [y|n]?`
   - In our flat, dedicated-adapter lab architecture, type `n` and press Enter. (VLANs are only needed when multiple logical networks share a single physical trunk port).
3. WAN Interface Assignment: `Enter the WAN interface name or 'a' for auto-detection: `
   - Type `em0` (or `vtnet0` if using VirtIO) and press Enter.
4. LAN Interface Assignment: `Enter the LAN interface name or 'a' for auto-detection: `
   - Type `em1` (or `vtnet1`) and press Enter.
5. Optional Interface 1 (OPT1): `Enter the Optional 1 interface name: `
   - Press Enter to skip for now (we assign OPT1/OPT2 cleanly via Menu Option 1 or the webGUI).
6. Confirmation: pfSense displays the proposed mapping and asks `Do you want to proceed [y|n]?` Type `y` and press Enter.
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| pfSense Initial Console Setup Wizard                                  |
|                                                                       |
|  Valid interfaces found:                                              |
|  em0   08:00:27:11:22:01   (Adapter 1 - VirtualBox NAT)               |
|  em1   08:00:27:11:22:02   (Adapter 2 - Internal sxl-lan)             |
|  em2   08:00:27:11:22:03   (Adapter 3 - Internal sxl-dmz)             |
|  em3   08:00:27:11:22:04   (Adapter 4 - Internal sxl-mgmt)            |
|                                                                       |
|  Should VLANs be set up now [y|n]? n                                  |
|  Enter the WAN interface name: em0                                    |
|  Enter the LAN interface name: em1                                    |
|  Enter the Optional 1 interface name or 'a' for auto-detection: [Enter]|
|                                                                       |
|  Proceed with changes [y|n]? y                                        |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In an enterprise data center with multi-port 10GbE fiber cards, administrators must match MAC addresses displayed on the console with physical cable switchport patch schedules. Getting the WAN and LAN interfaces backwards exposes internal networks directly to the Internet.
concepts.configurationRelevance: Answering `n` to VLANs and correctly assigning `em0` to WAN and `em1` to LAN establishes the baseline configuration necessary for pfSense to start its web server and DHCP daemon.
concepts.verification: After answering `y`, the system writes the initial `/cf/conf/config.xml` file, configures interfaces, starts daemons, and renders the standard 16-option pfSense console menu.
commonMistakes: Answering 'y' to the VLAN prompt, leading down an unnecessary series of VLAN tag and parent interface questions.
Swapping WAN and LAN (assigning `em1` to WAN and `em0` to LAN), which prevents the LAN workstation from receiving an IP via DHCP.
Typing 'a' for auto-detection in VirtualBox, which requires physically unplugging and plugging virtual cables to detect link state changes.
concepts.troubleshooting: If you misconfigure the interfaces during initial boot, do not panic. Once the 16-option console menu appears, select Option 1 ('Assign Interfaces') to reassign interfaces at any time.
keyTakeaways: Always enter 'n' for VLANs during basic multi-adapter lab setups.
em0 maps to WAN (Adapter 1) and em1 maps to LAN (Adapter 2).
pfSense writes the initial configuration to config.xml upon completion.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should you enter at the initial pfSense console prompt: 'Should VLANs be set up now [y|n]?' for our four-adapter lab?
options: Type 'n' and press Enter, because we have four dedicated virtual network adapters and do not require 802.1Q trunking.
Type 'y' and press Enter to create 4 VLANs on adapter 1.
Type 'a' to let pfSense automatically detect the VLANs.
Press Ctrl+C to abort the setup wizard.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: Because each security zone connects to its own dedicated virtual adapter (Adapters 1-4), 802.1Q VLAN tagging is not needed. Typing 'n' allows clean 1-to-1 physical interface assignment.

concepts.purpose: Explain the first-boot console prompts and proper interface assignment in pfSense.
howItWorks: Maps FreeBSD kernel interface drivers to initial WAN and LAN roles.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Essential first-boot step to transition from install to configuration.

concepts.title: Console Menu Option 1: Assign Interfaces (WAN, LAN, OPT1/DMZ, OPT2/MGMT)
learningObjectives: Navigate the 16-option pfSense console menu.
Use Console Option 1 ('Assign Interfaces') to map all four physical interfaces.
Assign em0 to WAN, em1 to LAN, em2 to OPT1 (DMZ), and em3 to OPT2 (MGMT).
concepts.conceptIntroduction: The pfSense text console menu is the primary out-of-band management interface. If the webGUI becomes unreachable or if interface cabling is altered, administrators can interact with the firewall via this menu. Option 1 allows administrators to assign, reorder, or add network interfaces to the system configuration without needing web browser access.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The pfSense console menu presents 16 standard management actions:
```
 0) Logout (SSH only)                  9) pfTop
 1) Assign Interfaces                10) Filter Logs
 2) Set interface(s) IP address       11) Restart webConfigurator
 3) Reset webConfigurator password    12) PHP shell + pfSense tools
 4) Reset to factory defaults         13) Update from console
 5) Reboot system                     14) Enable Secure Shell (sshd)
 6) Halt system                       15) Restore recent configuration
 7) Ping host                         16) Restart PHP-FPM
 8) Shell
```
To assign all four interfaces using Option 1:
1. Type `1` and press Enter.
2. VLAN prompt: `Should VLANs be set up now [y|n]?` -> Type `n` and press Enter.
3. WAN interface: Type `em0` and press Enter.
4. LAN interface: Type `em1` and press Enter.
5. Optional 1 (OPT1) interface: Type `em2` and press Enter.
6. Optional 2 (OPT2) interface: Type `em3` and press Enter.
7. Optional 3 interface: Press Enter to finish assignment.
8. Confirmation: Review the mapping:
   - `WAN  -> em0`
   - `LAN  -> em1`
   - `OPT1 -> em2`
   - `OPT2 -> em3`
   Type `y` and press Enter to save and apply.
concepts.enterpriseExample: In enterprise incident response, if an administrator accidentally creates a firewall rule that blocks all access to the LAN interface, physical access to the console (or hypervisor VMRC/IPMI KVM) allows the admin to use Option 1 to quickly reassign administration to a secondary port.
concepts.configurationRelevance: Option 1 registers all four interfaces in pfSense's database, making OPT1 and OPT2 visible in both the console and the webGUI under Interfaces -> (assign).
concepts.verification:
The console menu updates its top banner to show all four interfaces:
- `WAN (wan) -> em0 -> v4/DHCP4: 10.0.2.15/24`
- `LAN (lan) -> em1 -> v4: 192.168.1.1/24 (default, will be updated to 10.10.10.1/24)`
- `OPT1 (opt1) -> em2 -> (none)`
- `OPT2 (opt2) -> em3 -> (none)`
commonMistakes: Pressing Enter on OPT1 without typing `em2`, skipping interface assignment for DMZ.
Reversing em2 and em3, causing DMZ rules to inadvertently apply to the MGMT interface.
Accidentally typing `y` to the VLAN prompt during Option 1 execution.
concepts.troubleshooting: If the banner does not show OPT1 or OPT2, run Option 1 again. Ensure you type `em2` for Optional 1 and `em3` for Optional 2 before pressing Enter.
keyTakeaways: Console Option 1 configures the mapping between hardware drivers and logical firewall interfaces.
All four interfaces (em0 through em3) must be assigned to support our multi-zone topology.
The console menu banner immediately reflects the active interface mappings.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which pfSense console menu option is used to assign network interface cards to WAN, LAN, and OPT interfaces?
options: Option 1 (Assign Interfaces)
Option 2 (Set interface(s) IP address)
Option 4 (Reset to factory defaults)
Option 8 (Shell)
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: Option 1 is specifically designated for interface assignment. Option 2 sets IP addresses, Option 4 resets configuration, and Option 8 opens the FreeBSD Unix shell.

concepts.purpose: Instruct students on using pfSense console Option 1 to assign all 4 network interfaces.
howItWorks: Modifies the interface configuration elements in config.xml.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Ensures all 4 security zones are recognized by the firewall kernel.

concepts.title: Console Menu Option 2: Set Interface IP Addresses for LAN (10.10.10.1/24) and Built-in DHCP
learningObjectives: Use Console Option 2 to reconfigure the LAN IP address from default 192.168.1.1/24 to 10.10.10.1/24.
Configure the CIDR prefix length (24) and understand why no upstream gateway is entered for LAN.
Enable and configure the built-in DHCP server range (10.10.10.100 to 10.10.10.200) and revert HTTP/HTTPS settings.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: By default, pfSense assigns `192.168.1.1/24` to its LAN interface. In modern enterprise environments and home lab setups, the `192.168.1.0/24` subnet frequently conflicts with consumer home routers or corporate Wi-Fi gateways. Console Option 2 allows administrators to reconfigure the LAN IP address to our enterprise standard `10.10.10.1/24` and adjust the built-in DHCP server range so LAN clients automatically receive proper IP configurations.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The detailed execution steps for Option 2 are:
1. From the console menu, type `2` and press Enter.
2. Interface Selection: Enter `2` (corresponding to LAN) and press Enter.
3. IPv4 Address: `Enter the new LAN IPv4 address: ` -> Type `10.10.10.1` and press Enter.
4. Subnet Bit Count: `Enter the new LAN IPv4 subnet bit count (1 to 32): ` -> Type `24` (equivalent to 255.255.255.0) and press Enter.
5. Upstream Gateway: `For a WAN, enter the new LAN IPv4 upstream gateway address. For a LAN, press <ENTER> for none: ` -> Press Enter! (CRITICAL: LAN has NO upstream gateway; pfSense IS the gateway).
6. IPv6 Address: `Enter the new LAN IPv6 address: ` -> Press Enter to skip.
7. DHCP Server: `Do you want to enable the DHCP server on LAN [y|n]?` -> Type `y` and press Enter.
8. DHCP Start Address: `Enter the start address of the IPv4 client address range: ` -> Type `10.10.10.100` and press Enter.
9. DHCP End Address: `Enter the end address of the IPv4 client address range: ` -> Type `10.10.10.200` and press Enter.
10. Revert to HTTP: `Do you want to revert to HTTP as the webConfigurator protocol [y|n]?` -> Type `n` (keep HTTPS enabled for encrypted webGUI access).
11. Completion: The console updates the webConfigurator URL to `https://10.10.10.1`.
concepts.enterpriseExample: In enterprise branch office provisioning, local interfaces are assigned specific subnets designated by network architecture teams. Entering an upstream gateway on an internal interface corrupts the kernel default routing table, redirecting external Internet traffic back into the internal network.
concepts.configurationRelevance: Setting 10.10.10.1/24 and enabling DHCP allows client VMs attached to the 'sxl-lan' Internal Network to boot up, automatically obtain an IP, configure 10.10.10.1 as default gateway, and immediately open the webGUI.
concepts.verification: Check the console menu header: Confirm `LAN (lan) -> em1 -> v4: 10.10.10.1/24`. On a client connected to `sxl-lan`, run `ip addr` to verify it received an IP in the 10.10.10.100-200 range.
commonMistakes: Entering an upstream gateway address (such as 10.10.10.1 or 192.168.1.1) on the LAN interface, which overwrites the default route and breaks WAN routing.
Entering a subnet mask in dotted-decimal format (255.255.255.0) instead of bit count (24).
Setting the DHCP range outside the subnet (e.g. 192.168.1.100) or overlapping with the firewall's IP (10.10.10.1).
concepts.troubleshooting: If Internet routing fails immediately after configuring LAN, check Diagnostics -> Routes. If LAN is listed as default gateway instead of WAN, re-run Option 2 and press Enter when asked for the upstream gateway.
keyTakeaways: LAN interfaces NEVER have an upstream gateway configured.
Subnet masks are specified as bit count (24 for 255.255.255.0).
Enabling DHCP on LAN automates client IP configuration for rapid lab onboarding.

knowledgeCheck.question: When configuring the LAN interface in pfSense Console Option 2, what should you enter for 'LAN IPv4 upstream gateway address'?
options: Press Enter for none (LAN interfaces do not have an upstream gateway; the firewall is the gateway for LAN clients)
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: Only WAN interfaces connecting to upstream transit providers have upstream gateways. Specifying an upstream gateway on an internal LAN interface breaks the firewall's default routing table.

concepts.purpose: Guide students through setting LAN IP 10.10.10.1/24 and DHCP pool via Console Option 2.
howItWorks: Updates interface IPv4 address, subnet mask, and starts the dhcpd service.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Enables client access to the pfSense web configuration portal.

concepts.title: Creating the Client Test VMs: Attaching Workstations and Servers to Internal Networks
learningObjectives: Provision a lightweight test VM (Ubuntu, Debian, or Alpine Linux) to serve as a LAN test client.
Attach the client VM's virtual network adapter to the 'sxl-lan' Internal Network.
Verify dynamic IP acquisition from pfSense's DHCP server and test gateway ping reachability.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: A firewall cannot be meaningfully tested without endpoints generating traffic across its security zones. To test our multi-zone policy in Session 4, we provision at least one lightweight client virtual machine (such as an Ubuntu Desktop or Debian Linux VM) connected to the LAN zone (`sxl-lan`), and optionally a second VM in the DMZ zone (`sxl-dmz`) representing a web server.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
To configure a LAN test client VM in VirtualBox:
1. VM Creation: Create a VM named `sxl-lan-client01` (1-2 GB RAM, 1 vCPU, lightweight Linux OS).
2. Adapter Attachment: In VM Settings -> Network -> Adapter 1:
   - Attached to: `Internal Network`
   - Name: `sxl-lan` (Must match pfSense Adapter 2 name exactly!)
   - Promiscuous Mode: `Allow VMs`
3. Client Boot & DHCP: Boot the client VM. The operating system's network manager sends a DHCP Discover broadcast on the virtual switch.
4. IP Acquisition: pfSense's DHCP server listens on `em1` (10.10.10.1) and responds with an IP lease (e.g. 10.10.10.100), subnet mask (255.255.255.0), default gateway (10.10.10.1), and DNS server (10.10.10.1 / pfSense Unbound DNS resolver).
5. Connectivity Test: On the client, open a terminal and execute `ip addr show` to verify the IP lease, followed by `ping 10.10.10.1` to confirm Layer 3 reachability to the firewall gateway.
concepts.enterpriseExample: In enterprise deployment rollouts, staging test clients in isolated testing VLANs allows security engineers to validate DHCP option delivery (such as Option 43 for wireless controllers or Option 66 for VoIP phones) without affecting production user segments.
concepts.configurationRelevance: Without this client VM attached to `sxl-lan`, you cannot open a web browser to configure the pfSense webConfigurator, because the host computer cannot reach the private `sxl-lan` internal network directly.
concepts.verification:
From the client VM terminal, execute:
- `ip route`: Verify `default via 10.10.10.1 dev eth0` is present.
- `ping -c 3 10.10.10.1`: Verify 0% packet loss to the pfSense LAN interface.
- `curl -I https://10.10.10.1 -k`: Verify pfSense web server returns HTTP 200/302 response.
commonMistakes: Leaving the client adapter set to 'NAT', giving it a 10.0.2.x IP from VirtualBox rather than an IP from pfSense.
Typo in the Internal Network name (e.g. `sxllan` instead of `sxl-lan`), isolating the client on an empty virtual switch.
Client firewall (iptables/ufw or Windows Defender) blocking ICMP responses during initial ping tests.
concepts.troubleshooting: If the client VM does not receive an IP, run `sudo dhclient -v eth0` (or `sudo systemctl restart networking`). If it times out waiting for DHCPOFFER, verify the Internal Network name matches pfSense exactly.
keyTakeaways: Client VMs must connect to the same named Internal Network as pfSense's LAN interface.
pfSense provides DHCP addresses and acts as default gateway.
Management access to pfSense occurs from within the LAN or MGMT virtual machines.

knowledgeCheck.question: If a test client VM in VirtualBox cannot acquire an IP address from pfSense's DHCP server, which setting should you check first?
options: Verify that the client VM's network adapter is set to 'Internal Network' and the network name matches pfSense's LAN network name ('sxl-lan') exactly.
Reinstall the client VM's operating system.
Change the client VM's RAM allocation.
Reboot the physical host computer.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: VirtualBox Internal Networks isolate traffic by name. If the names do not match identically, the VMs are plugged into different virtual switches and cannot exchange DHCP broadcast packets.

concepts.purpose: Instruct on configuring test client virtual machines attached to the internal lab networks.
howItWorks: Binds client virtual NICs to the hypervisor internal switch bus.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Provides the student workstation needed to administer and test the firewall.

concepts.title: First webGUI Login: Accessing https://10.10.10.1, Handling TLS Certificates, and Default Credentials
learningObjectives: Access the pfSense webConfigurator from the LAN client browser at https://10.10.10.1.
Understand why web browsers display a 'Your connection is not private' TLS warning and safely proceed.
Log in using the default administrative credentials (username: admin, password: pfsense).
concepts.conceptIntroduction: The primary management interface for pfSense is its webConfigurator—a secure, web-based graphical administrative console served over HTTPS. On initial connection, every modern browser presents a security certificate warning because pfSense generates a self-signed TLS certificate during installation. Understanding why this occurs and knowing the factory credentials allows administrators to safely access the console.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The login process involves:
1. URL Navigation: Open a web browser on the LAN client VM and navigate to `https://10.10.10.1`.
2. TLS Certificate Validation: The browser inspects the TLS certificate returned by the pfSense web server (lighttpd/nginx). Because the certificate was self-generated by pfSense rather than signed by a globally trusted Certificate Authority (such as Let's Encrypt or DigiCert), the browser displays `NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID` or `MOZILLA_PKIX_ERROR_SELF_SIGNED_CER`.
3. Certificate Bypass: Click 'Advanced' (or 'Show Details') and select 'Accept the Risk and Continue' (or 'Proceed to 10.10.10.1 (unsafe)'). In a private lab or enterprise management environment, this is standard procedure for initial self-signed device certificates.
4. Authentication: The login screen appears with the Netgate pfSense logo. Enter:
   - Username: `admin`
   - Password: `pfsense` (all lowercase)
5. Session Establishment: pfSense validates credentials against its local user database (`/cf/conf/config.xml`), creates an encrypted session cookie, and automatically launches the Setup Wizard on first login.
concepts.enterpriseExample: In production enterprise networks, network appliances are provisioned with certificates issued by an internal Enterprise Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) such as Microsoft Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS). In training labs, self-signed certificates provide identical wire encryption.
concepts.configurationRelevance: The default password `pfsense` represents a severe security vulnerability. The setup wizard immediately forces the administrator to replace this credential with a hardened enterprise passphrase.
concepts.verification: After entering `admin` / `pfsense`, verify the browser redirects to `https://10.10.10.1/wizard.php?xml=setup_wizard.xml` and displays 'Netgate pfSense Setup'.
commonMistakes: Attempting to connect via plain `http://10.10.10.1` when HTTPS is enforced, which may result in connection refused or automatic redirection.
Capitalizing the default credentials (e.g. typing `Admin` or `PfSense`), which fails because FreeBSD authentication is strictly case-sensitive.
Panicking at the browser certificate warning and aborting rather than clicking Advanced -> Proceed.
concepts.troubleshooting: If the login page fails to load, check if the client VM has an IP on 10.10.10.0/24. From the console menu on pfSense, choose Option 11 ('Restart webConfigurator') to reinitialize the web server service.
keyTakeaways: pfSense uses HTTPS with a self-signed certificate out-of-the-box.
Default factory credentials are username 'admin' and password 'pfsense'.
The browser certificate warning is normal for private management appliances using self-signed certs.

knowledgeCheck.question: What are the default administrative credentials for a fresh installation of pfSense Community Edition?
options: Username: admin, Password: pfsense
Username: root, Password: toor
Username: administrator, Password: password123
Username: admin, Password: (blank)
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: Netgate pfSense Community Edition ships with default username 'admin' and password 'pfsense' in lowercase.

concepts.purpose: Instruct on connecting to the pfSense webConfigurator and bypassing self-signed TLS warnings.
howItWorks: Initiates an encrypted TLS session and authenticates against the admin user database.
concepts.practicalRelevance: The entry point to all subsequent graphical firewall administration.

concepts.title: pfSense Setup Wizard Walkthrough: Hostname, Domain, DNS, NTP, and Hardened Admin Password
learningObjectives: Navigate the 9-step initial pfSense Setup Wizard.
Configure enterprise identity parameters (Hostname: sxl-pfsense-fw01, Domain: shadowxlab.local).
Set public upstream DNS servers (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) and synchronize time via NTP.
Change the default administrative password and reload the system configuration.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: The pfSense Setup Wizard is an interactive onboarding sequence that runs automatically upon first login. It guides administrators through establishing the firewall's network identity, upstream domain name resolution, clock synchronization, and foundational security hardening.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The Setup Wizard sequence consists of:
1. Step 1 & 2: Introduction and Netgate Global Support overview. Click 'Next'.
2. Step 3 (General Information):
   - Hostname: `sxl-pfsense-fw01`
   - Domain: `shadowxlab.local`
   - Primary DNS Server: `1.1.1.1` (Cloudflare DNS)
   - Secondary DNS Server: `8.8.8.8` (Google DNS)
   - DNS Resolution Behavior: Check 'Override DNS' (allows WAN DHCP to provide additional servers if needed)
3. Step 4 (Time Server Information):
   - Time Server (NTP): `2.pfsense.pool.ntp.org`
   - Timezone: Select your regional timezone (e.g. `UTC` or `Asia/Kolkata`)
4. Step 5 (Configure WAN Interface):
   - Selected Type: `DHCP` (Default for VirtualBox NAT)
   - Block RFC1918 Private Networks: UNCHECK this box for VirtualBox lab environments! (Because VirtualBox WAN is 10.0.2.x, which is RFC 1918. Leaving this checked blocks all inbound WAN traffic!).
   - Block bogon networks: UNCHECK for lab testing.
5. Step 6 (Configure LAN Interface):
   - Confirm LAN IP: `10.10.10.1`, Subnet Mask: `24`. Click 'Next'.
6. Step 7 (Set Admin Password):
   - Enter a hardened password (e.g. `ShadowXLab@2026!`), re-enter to confirm.
7. Step 8 (Reload Configuration):
   - Click 'Reload' to apply changes and restart affected system daemons.
8. Step 9 (Finish):
   - Click 'Finish' to enter the main pfSense dashboard.
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| pfSense Setup Wizard Key Decisions                                    |
|                                                                       |
|  Step 3: Identity & DNS                                               |
|  - Hostname: sxl-pfsense-fw01 | Domain: shadowxlab.local              |
|  - DNS Servers: 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8                                      |
|                                                                       |
|  Step 4: Time                                                         |
|  - NTP Server: 2.pfsense.pool.ntp.org | Timezone: Asia/Kolkata        |
|                                                                       |
|  Step 5: WAN Configuration (CRITICAL LAB SETTING)                     |
|  - Type: DHCP                                                         |
|  - [ ] Block RFC1918 Private Networks  <--- MUST UNCHECK FOR VBOX LAB |
|  - [ ] Block bogon networks            <--- MUST UNCHECK FOR VBOX LAB |
|                                                                       |
|  Step 7: Admin Hardening                                              |
|  - Set strong administrative passphrase                               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In an enterprise perimeter firewall, NTP time synchronization is legally critical for log forensics. If firewall event timestamps drift by even a few seconds, correlation between firewall deny logs and server breach logs becomes inadmissible in security incident audits.
concepts.configurationRelevance: The 'Block RFC1918 Private Networks' checkbox on WAN is enabled by default as a best practice for firewalls connected directly to public ISPs. In a hypervisor lab, however, VirtualBox's NAT network uses `10.0.2.0/24` (an RFC 1918 private range). Leaving this box checked causes pfSense to drop all WAN responses, breaking Internet access for the lab!
concepts.verification: After reloading, the dashboard opens. In the 'System Information' widget, verify Hostname displays `sxl-pfsense-fw01.shadowxlab.local` and the system clock matches your local time.
commonMistakes: Leaving 'Block RFC1918 Private Networks' checked on WAN during lab setup, breaking all outbound Internet connectivity for the entire lab.
Setting an administrative password and immediately forgetting it without recording it in lab notes.
Leaving the timezone set to default Etc/UTC when reviewing classroom logs, causing timestamp confusion.
concepts.troubleshooting: If the firewall cannot reach external websites after wizard completion, navigate to Interfaces -> WAN, scroll to the bottom, uncheck 'Block private networks and loopback addresses', click 'Save' and 'Apply Changes'.
keyTakeaways: The setup wizard configures host identity, DNS, and NTP synchronization.
Always uncheck 'Block RFC1918 Private Networks' on WAN in VirtualBox NAT lab environments.
Changing the default password hardens the management plane immediately.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why MUST the 'Block RFC1918 Private Networks' checkbox be UNCHECKED on the WAN interface in a VirtualBox lab environment?
options: Because VirtualBox NAT uses 10.0.2.0/24 (an RFC 1918 private range) for the WAN interface; keeping this option checked causes the firewall to drop all WAN traffic.
Because pfSense CE does not support RFC 1918 filtering.
Because checking the box permanently disables the webConfigurator.
Because VirtualBox will crash if RFC 1918 blocking is enabled.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: VirtualBox NAT assigns private RFC 1918 addresses (10.0.2.15) to virtual machines. If 'Block RFC1918' is active on WAN, pfSense treats all upstream traffic from the VirtualBox gateway as spoofed and drops it.

concepts.purpose: Walk through the pfSense Initial Setup Wizard with emphasis on critical lab settings.
howItWorks: Sets global configuration parameters and writes them to config.xml.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Establishes baseline system identity and prevents common lab WAN lockouts.

concepts.title: OPT1 Interface Setup: Enable, Rename to DMZ, Configure Static IPv4 (172.16.50.1/24), and Apply
learningObjectives: Navigate to Interfaces -> OPT1 in the pfSense webConfigurator.
Enable the interface and rename its descriptive alias to 'DMZ'.
Assign static IPv4 address 172.16.50.1 with /24 subnet mask and commit changes.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: When interfaces beyond WAN and LAN are added in pfSense, the system assigns them generic identifiers like OPT1, OPT2, etc. These interfaces start in a disabled state with no IP configuration. To establish our De-Militarized Zone (DMZ), administrators must enable OPT1, rename it to reflect its business role, and assign its designated static gateway address.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The configuration procedure for the DMZ interface:
1. Navigation: In the pfSense top navigation menu, click `Interfaces` -> `OPT1` (or Interfaces -> Assignments -> click on OPT1).

concepts.title: Snapshot Strategy: Taking Clean Baseline Snapshots in VirtualBox Before Configuration
learningObjectives: Understand how VirtualBox differencing disks and snapshots function.
Execute a clean shutdown and create a 'Baseline 4-Zone Configured' snapshot.
Know how to rapidly revert the virtual machine to a known-good baseline when misconfigurations occur.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: Firewall administration involves configuring complex rule sets where a single syntax error, misplaced blocking rule, or inverted interface setting can instantly lock administrators out of the firewall or disrupt routing. Hypervisor snapshots capture the exact disk and memory state of a virtual machine at a specific point in time, enabling instant recovery without reinstalling.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
VirtualBox snapshots operate using copy-on-write differencing hard disk images:
1. Base Disk Freezing: When a snapshot is taken, VirtualBox freezes the primary `.vdi` image into read-only mode.
2. Differencing Disk Creation: VirtualBox creates a new differencing `.vdi` file that records only sectors modified after the snapshot point.
3. Reversion: Restoring a snapshot discards the differencing disk, instantly returning the virtual hard drive to the exact sector state of the snapshot.

Recommended Lab Snapshot Procedure:
1. Graceful Shutdown: Inside pfSense webGUI, click Diagnostics -> Halt System (or Option 6 on the console) to flush all pending ZFS disk buffers cleanly to disk.
2. VirtualBox Snapshot Creation: In the VirtualBox main window, select `sxl-pfsense-fw01` -> Snapshots (camera icon) -> Click 'Take'.
3. Snapshot Metadata:
   - Name: `Snapshot 1: Clean 4-Zone Baseline`
   - Description: `pfSense 2.7.2 installed with ZFS. WAN (NAT), LAN (10.10.10.1/24), DMZ (172.16.50.1/24), MGMT (192.168.100.1/24). Admin password updated, Wizard completed.`
4. Power On: Start the VM and proceed safely to Session 4 rule configuration.

| Hypervisor Snapshot Architecture                                      |
|                                                                       |
|  [Base Virtual Hard Disk: sxl-pfsense-fw01.vdi]                       |
|  (FreeBSD OS, ZFS pool, initial pfSense base installation)            |
|                                                                       |
|  ============== TAKE SNAPSHOT 1: CLEAN BASELINE ==============        |
|                                                                       |
|  Base Disk frozen as READ-ONLY                                        |
|         |                                                             |
|         v                                                             |
|  [Differencing Disk: {uuid}.vdi] <--- All Session 4 Rule Changes Written|
|         |                                                             |
|         +----> If rule lockout occurs:                                |
|                Click 'Restore Snapshot 1'                             |
|                Differencing disk discarded                            |
|                Firewall instantly returns to clean 4-zone baseline!   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In enterprise change management (ITIL), creating virtual machine snapshots before applying firewall firmware updates or major policy refactors is a mandatory requirement. If an update causes kernel instability or breaks production routing, the change window rollback plan executes a snapshot restore in under two minutes.
concepts.configurationRelevance: Having this snapshot gives students the confidence to experiment aggressively with blocking rules, NAT redirects, and interface policies during Session 4 without fear of permanently destroying their lab setup.
concepts.verification: In VirtualBox, open the VM snapshots panel. Verify 'Snapshot 1: Clean 4-Zone Baseline' is listed in the tree directly above 'Current State'.
commonMistakes: Taking a snapshot while the VM is in an inconsistent state or actively writing to disk, which can occasionally cause filesystem replay errors.
Failing to enter descriptive snapshot names, leading to confusion when multiple unnamed snapshots accumulate.
Assuming snapshots replace long-term configuration backups (`config.xml` export).
concepts.troubleshooting: If you lock yourself out of the webGUI during firewall rule testing in Session 4, power off the VM, select 'Snapshot 1: Clean 4-Zone Baseline', click 'Restore', and power the VM back on.
keyTakeaways: Snapshots capture point-in-time virtual disk state using differencing images.
Taking a baseline snapshot after 4-zone configuration ensures risk-free lab experimentation.
Always shut down cleanly before taking baseline snapshots.

knowledgeCheck.question: What happens when you restore a VirtualBox snapshot on the pfSense virtual machine?
options: All disk changes made after the snapshot was taken are discarded, instantly reverting the firewall's configuration to the exact state saved in the snapshot.
The entire virtual machine is deleted from the hard drive.
VirtualBox merges all changes permanently into the base disk.
pfSense resets its administrative password to default.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: Restoring a snapshot discards changes written to the differencing disk since the snapshot was captured, rolling the system back to the known-good configuration baseline.

concepts.purpose: Instruct students on hypervisor snapshot strategies for safe firewall rule experimentation.
howItWorks: Freezes base virtual disk and redirects writes to a differencing image.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Essential safety net before implementing restrictive firewall rules.

concepts.title: Troubleshooting Lab Connectivity: Common VirtualBox and pfSense Installation Pitfalls
learningObjectives: Diagnose and resolve the top five most common virtual firewall lab connectivity failures.
Troubleshoot VirtualBox internal network mismatches and missing adapter attachments.
Resolve IP addressing conflicts, default route anomalies, and administrative lockout scenarios.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: Virtual firewall laboratories are complex environments combining hypervisor virtual networking, BSD kernel drivers, and firewall filtering engines. When connectivity fails, beginner administrators often struggle to pinpoint whether the fault lies in VirtualBox settings, client operating system network configurations, or pfSense firewall rules. Following a systematic Layer 1 to Layer 4 diagnostic process rapidly isolates and resolves the fault.
concepts.technicalExplanation:
The Systematic Troubleshooting Workflow:
1. Hypervisor Verification (Layer 1/2):
   - Problem: Client cannot ping 10.10.10.1 or obtain DHCP IP.
   - Check: In VirtualBox VM settings for BOTH pfSense and client, verify Adapter 2 on pfSense and Adapter 1 on client are set to 'Internal Network' with the EXACT string `sxl-lan`.
   - Check: Verify 'Cable Connected' checkbox is checked on both VMs.
2. Client IP Verification (Layer 3):
   - Problem: Client displays an APIPA address (`169.254.x.x`) or 0.0.0.0.
   - Fix: Release and renew DHCP lease (`sudo dhclient -r && sudo dhclient -v eth0` on Linux, `ipconfig /release && ipconfig /renew` on Windows).
   - Check: Confirm client subnet mask is `255.255.255.0` (/24) and default gateway is `10.10.10.1`.
3. Firewall Routing Verification (Layer 3 Routing):
   - Problem: pfSense cannot ping external Internet IPs (e.g. 8.8.8.8).
   - Check: In pfSense webGUI under Diagnostics -> Routes, verify `default` points to VirtualBox NAT gateway (`10.0.2.2`).
   - Check: Ensure 'Block RFC1918 Private Networks' is unchecked on WAN.
4. Administrative Lockout Recovery (Management Access):
   - Problem: Administrator accidentally locked out of webGUI via bad firewall rule.
   - Recovery 1: From the pfSense console menu, type `8` to open shell, and run `pfctl -d` to temporarily disable packet filtering (`pfctl -e` re-enables it).
   - Recovery 2: From console menu, run Option 15 ('Restore recent configuration') to roll back the last `config.xml` edit.
   - Recovery 3: Revert to VirtualBox Baseline Snapshot.

|                                                                       |
|  Level 1: Hypervisor Layer                                            |
|  [Are both VMs attached to 'Internal Network' with IDENTICAL names?]  |
|  [Is 'Cable Connected' checked in VirtualBox?]                        |
|        | YES                                                          |
|        v                                                              |
|  Level 2: IP Configuration Layer                                      |
|  [Does client have a valid 10.10.10.x/24 IP?]                         |
|  [Is default gateway set to 10.10.10.1?]                              |
|        | YES                                                          |
|        v                                                              |
|  Level 3: Gateway Reachability Layer                                  |
|  [Can client ping 10.10.10.1?]                                        |
|  [Can pfSense ping 10.0.2.2 (VirtualBox WAN NAT Gateway)?]            |
|        | YES                                                          |
|        v                                                              |
|  Level 4: Firewall Policy & Service Layer                             |
|  [Is webConfigurator service running (Option 11)?]                    |
|  [Is packet filter blocking traffic? (pfctl -d to test)]              |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In Network Operations Centers (NOC), engineers follow the OSI model bottom-up when responding to outages: checking physical link lights, then Layer 2 MAC tables, then Layer 3 ARP and routing tables, and finally Layer 4 ACLs and services.
concepts.configurationRelevance: The `pfctl -d` console shell command is the ultimate safety tool for firewall administrators. It disables packet filtering in the FreeBSD kernel without stopping the routing engine or webGUI, allowing immediate recovery from accidental lockout rules.
concepts.verification: Test the diagnostic commands from the console shell: run `pfctl -s info` to verify packet filter state, and `netstat -rn` to display the active routing table.
commonMistakes: Assuming a network issue is a firewall rule failure before verifying hypervisor adapter attachment and cable connect status.
Attempting to ping WAN IPs before verifying the WAN interface has acquired an IP from VirtualBox NAT.
Reinstalling pfSense when a simple `pfctl -d` from the console would resolve a lockout.
concepts.troubleshooting: If locked out of pfSense, open the VirtualBox VM console window, press 8 for Shell, type `pfctl -d` and press Enter. Access https://10.10.10.1 in your browser, fix the rule, and run `pfctl -e` to re-enable protection.
keyTakeaways: Troubleshoot systematically from Hypervisor -> IP -> Routing -> Firewall Policy.
Matching Internal Network names is the #1 prerequisite for virtual lab connectivity.
Use 'pfctl -d' from console shell to temporarily disable firewall filtering during lockouts.

knowledgeCheck.question: If you accidentally apply a firewall rule that blocks all access to the pfSense webConfigurator from your LAN client, which console shell command temporarily disables packet filtering so you can log back in?
options: pfctl -d
systemctl stop firewall
iptables -F
killall lighttpd
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Option A is correct: In FreeBSD/pfSense, `pfctl -d` disables the PF (Packet Filter) engine immediately. Once logged back into the webGUI, you can correct the misconfigured rule and run `pfctl -e` to re-enable filtering.

concepts.purpose: Provide a comprehensive troubleshooting guide for common virtual firewall lab failures.
howItWorks: Establishes an OSI-aligned diagnostic workflow and emergency recovery tools.
concepts.practicalRelevance: Crucial survival skill for troubleshooting lab deadlocks and lockouts.

concepts.title: How pfSense Evaluates Firewall Rules: Top-to-Bottom, First-Match Wins, and Implicit Default Deny
learningObjectives: Understand the top-to-bottom, first-match evaluation logic of pfSense interface firewall rules.
Explain why rule positioning directly determines packet fate.
Understand the invisible implicit default deny rule operating at the bottom of every interface ruleset.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: Firewall rules in pfSense Community Edition do not operate as a collective aggregate; they are evaluated as an ordered, sequential list from top to bottom.
